extracted.intended_audience: readers and scholars of Renaissance satire / Rabelais (general readers of humorous classical literature)
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from Rabelais' Gargantua and Pantagruel (chapters on governance, household economy, and the praise/heresy of debt), presenting prescriptive and satirical maxims about rulers, thrift, debt, and social order. The passage mixes genuine political/philosophical prescriptions with Panurge's comic, inverted defenses of extravagance and indebtedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good ruler / king characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: A king rules not merely by force but by easing the people of their troubles, teaching them how to live well, honestly giving them good laws, and using them with affability, courtesy, gentleness, and liberality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Osiris, Alexander, Hercules: relieve people from oppressions and exactions; govern with discretion; maintain equity and justice; establish religion and wholesome laws suited to soil, climate, and disposition; supply what is wanting and abate the superfluous; pardon past offences and grant amnesties to secure goodwill and affection of the people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royal virtue: do always good and never ill
rubrics_metrics.description: Doing always good and never evil is presented as the singularly royal act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Based on Hesiod's idea of good demons (intercessors) who continually do good and protect from evil; used as a standard by which rulers/executives should be judged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of valour and justice
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful sovereign combines valour (shown in victory/conquest) with justice (shown in laws and the people's goodwill).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valour secures territory; justice secures consent. Quoted/illustrated with Virgil's line (Victorque volentes Per populos dat jura) and examples of rulers whose justice underpinned their authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect boundaries; avoid unjust conquest
rubrics_metrics.description: Frontiers and bounds of kingdoms should be guarded and preserved in peace and meekness; unjust or violent acquisition (blood and robbery) brings scandal and causes gains to perish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Numa's ordinance to Terminus and maxims like 'male parta, male dilabuntur' and 'de male quaesitis vix gaudet tertius haeres' to show moral and reputational penalties for unjust acquisition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Household-economy virtues (satirical mapping by Panurge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Panurge defends his profligacy by recasting various classical virtues as justifications for extravagant household conduct: prudence in borrowing beforehand; commutative justice in buying dear on trust and selling cheap; distributive justice in hospitable entertainment; fortitude in cutting down forests; temperance in eating corn while it is still blade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each 'virtue' is given an ironic example: borrowing as foresight (who knows how long the world lasts), buying dear/selling cheap as a path to becoming a perpetual seller (Cato), entertaining 'good fellows' and young women as distributive justice, felling trees to remove dens for criminals as fortitude, and consuming green corn as temperance and a way to save on laborers and processors. The passage supplies vivid, humorous justifications and bodily/medical 'benefits' of eating corn in the blade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roman sumptuary laws limiting expenditure
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to Roman laws (Orchia, Fannia, Didia, Licinia, Cornelia, Lepidiana, Antia, of the Corinthians) that forbade spending in one year more than one's annual revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These laws are cited as a historical institutional counterpoint to Panurge's extravagance; the text also mentions the Roman practice of Protervia (a sacrificial overeating) as a cultural contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Debt as social glue and a praised condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Panurge praises being indebted: continual indebtedness ensures that one always has people to pray for and flatter you; creditors become sources of social ties and support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments include social reciprocity (creditors will speak well of you to preserve their chance of repayment), religious/practical examples (servants burned at funerals had incentive to keep masters alive), and rhetorical celebration of creditors as 'flatterers' and 'parasites' who confer status. Panurge elevates debt to cosmic importance (the 'great soul of the universe').

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of a world without lending
rubrics_metrics.description: A hypothetical world with no lending or borrowing would descend into cosmic and social disorder—planets would rebel, elements would not transmute, mutual assistance would vanish, and human society would become predatory and anarchic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text elaborates a vivid chain of consequences: celestial disharmony (Jupiter vs Saturn), collapse of elemental cycles, cessation of mutual bodily functions as metaphor, and social breakdown into thieves and murderers. This is used to justify the necessity of lending for harmony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid debt; owe only love and mutual benevolence
rubrics_metrics.description: Pantagruel's counter-position: one should avoid owing money; one should not owe anything except love, friendship, and mutual benevolence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pantagruel invokes the Apostle and Plato: prefer self-sufficiency and labor over habitual borrowing; allow borrowing only when the diligent cannot provide by honest labour or through sudden mischance. The passage thus sets a prudential limit on Panurge's praise of debt.
